summary: Extends WebDAV to define a standard way of accessing, managing and sharing calendar and scheduling data in the iCalendar format. This document defines the calendar-access feature.

eli5.summary: A calendar lives on a server. CalDAV is a common language so different calendar apps can read, add and share events there, like using the same shared wall calendar.

questions: how to sync calendar with a server
how does caldav sync use etags
what is the caldav free busy report
subtitle: A standard way for calendar apps to store, query and share iCalendar data on a WebDAV server.

tldr.problem: Several companies had built calendar access over HTTP and WebDAV, but their products did not interoperate because each made different choices about how to model calendar data as WebDAV resources.
tldr.mechanism: CalDAV models each calendar as a WebDAV collection of iCalendar resources, adds collection properties, a MKCALENDAR method and a few REPORT queries, and requires ACLs, ETags and TLS support.
tldr.outcome: Clients can create calendars, store events, query by time range and sync through ETags with any compliant server. RFC 4791 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by several later RFCs.

today: RFC 4791 is a Proposed Standard that has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5689, RFC 6638, RFC 6764, RFC 7809, RFC 7953 and RFC 8996.

sections.title: What CalDAV Adds to WebDAV
sections.content:
Using HTTP and WebDAV as the basis for calendar access had been discussed in the IETF as early as 1997 or 1998. Several companies had implemented calendar access by uploading and downloading iCalendar objects over HTTP, and using WebDAV to list resources. Those implementations did not interoperate, because there were many decisions to make about how to model calendar data as WebDAV resources and about features WebDAV lacks. RFC 4791 proposes one model and adds the missing features. It defines the calendar-access feature of CalDAV.

To advertise CalDAV support, a server MUST support iCalendar as a media type for calendar object resources, WebDAV Class 1, WebDAV ACL (RFC 3744) with one added privilege, transport over TLS, ETags with extra rules, and all the calendaring reports. It SHOULD support the MKCALENDAR method. A server shows support by including calendar-access in the DAV header of an OPTIONS response.
sections.eli5: Different calendar programs each stored events in their own way and could not share. CalDAV picks one way and everyone follows it.

sections.title: Calendar Collections and Calendar Object Resources
sections.content:
A CalDAV calendar is a WebDAV collection (a folder) with a defined structure. Each item inside is a calendar object resource: an event, to-do, journal entry or other calendar component. Each can be locked and have its own WebDAV properties. The server is the canonical location for calendar data, and clients MUST be prepared for the data to change between synchronizations.

A calendar object resource MUST NOT contain more than one type of component (such as VEVENT or VTODO), apart from the VTIMEZONE components it needs, and MUST NOT specify the iCalendar METHOD property. The UID must be unique within the collection. All components that share a UID go in one resource, so a recurring event and its overridden instances are stored together. This keeps recurrence out of the count of resources and means less to synchronize.

A calendar collection can contain only calendar object resources and ordinary collections, and calendar collections MUST NOT be nested at any depth. Its DAV:resourcetype reports both DAV:collection and CALDAV:calendar.
sections.eli5: A calendar is a folder, and each event is its own file. An event that repeats, plus its changed dates, goes in one file.

sections.title: Calendar Collection Properties
sections.content:
CalDAV defines properties on calendar collections that describe and restrict what they hold. A server that has a limit tells the client through these properties, and storing anything beyond a limit fails with a matching precondition error.

  • calendar-description: a human-readable description.
  • calendar-timezone: the time zone the server uses to resolve dates and floating times.
  • supported-calendar-component-set and supported-calendar-data: the allowed component types and media types. Without the latter, only text/calendar iCalendar version 2.0 is accepted.
  • max-resource-size, min-date-time, max-date-time, max-instances and max-attendees-per-instance: size, date and recurrence limits.

A separate property on a user's principal resource, calendar-home-set, lists the URLs of the collections that contain that user's calendars. The CALDAV:read-free-busy privilege lets someone see busy times without seeing event details.
sections.eli5: Each calendar can carry a little sign saying what it is for and what it will accept, such as the biggest file or how far into the future.

sections.title: Creating Calendars and Events
sections.content:
The MKCALENDAR method creates a calendar collection. A server SHOULD support it but need not, because some stores give each user one pre-created calendar. A request can set properties such as DAV:displayname and calendar-description in its body, and either all instructions succeed or all are undone. A successful request returns 201 Created.

Events are created with an ordinary HTTP PUT of text/calendar data. Sending If-None-Match: * creates a new event, and changing an existing one uses If-Match with its ETag. Several preconditions apply to PUT, COPY and MOVE, including valid iCalendar data, a supported component type, no UID conflict and the collection's size, date and instance limits.

Every calendar object resource MUST have a strong ETag in DAV:getetag, returned on GET. A server SHOULD return a strong ETag on PUT only when the stored data is octet-for-octet what the client sent.
sections.eli5: To start a new calendar you ask the server to make one. To add an event you hand over a file, and the server gives it a version tag so everyone can tell if it changed.

sections.title: Searching with Reports
sections.content:
CalDAV uses the WebDAV REPORT method for queries. A server MUST support three reports.

calendar-query finds resources that match a filter. A filter can match component and property names, text (substring matches; the collations i;ascii-casemap and i;octet MUST be supported) and a time range, where the server MUST expand recurring components to see if any instance overlaps. The client chooses which properties and parts of the calendar data to get back. It can ask for only the master and relevant overridden components, or for each instance expanded, which helps clients that cannot compute recurrence. Answers come as a 207 Multi-Status response.

calendar-multiget fetches specific resources named by a list of DAV:href elements. free-busy-query takes one time range and returns a single VFREEBUSY component with busy periods, built from events the user may read or may read free-busy for. It carries busy time only; free time can be inferred. Periods of the same type SHOULD be coalesced.
sections.eli5: Instead of downloading the whole calendar, you can ask 'what is on during this week?', 'give me these three events', or 'when is this person busy?'.

sections.title: Synchronizing and Finding Calendars
sections.content:
The guidelines suggest that clients ask only for the time span on screen and sync only the present and near future, since history rarely changes. To sync, the client caches each resource's URI and ETag along with its data. It sends a calendar-query for the time range asking only for DAV:getetag, compares the ETags with its cache, then fetches the changed or new resources with calendar-multiget.

To change an event, a client has to PUT the whole resource, as there is no way to change individual properties incrementally. WebDAV locks can also protect an event while a user edits it, and the client should choose a short lock timeout when it locks automatically.

A client usually learns a calendar location from a URL the user gives it. Otherwise it can use a DAV:principal-match report to read calendar-home-set on its own principal, and a DAV:principal-property-search report to find another user's calendars.
sections.eli5: Your app keeps a copy and a version tag for each event. It asks which tags changed and only fetches those events.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
HTTP Basic authentication MUST NOT be used unless TLS is in effect. Servers MUST guard against reports that eat excessive CPU, memory or disk. The RFC gives the example of an event recurring every second for the next 100 years, which would produce approximately 3 x 10^9 instances.

Clients MUST NOT choose resource names that reveal data inside the event or the nature of a collection. Coalescing adjacent or overlapping busy periods of the same type in free-busy answers is the conservative privacy choice, since separate periods reveal at least two events. Procedure alarms are a known risk, and clients and servers are not required to execute them.
sections.eli5: Use a locked connection so nobody can peek. The server must not let one silly request make it work forever, and names of events should not give away secrets.
